subject: Is canned tuna healthy? Your weekly guide
title: PescoDial weekly guide
preheader: Plus a 20-minute garlic shrimp and white bean dinner, and a tip for canned beans.

intro.h1: Canned tuna, garlic shrimp and a pantry tip
paragraphs: Happy Sunday. This week's question is one I hear a lot: is that can of tuna in your pantry actually good for you?
The short answer is yes, for most people. But the kind of tuna and the salt on the label make a real difference, so I've pulled out the parts worth knowing.
Below you'll also find an easy shrimp dinner and one small tip for your next trip to the store.

question.question: Is canned tuna healthy?
question.answer: For most people, yes. Canned tuna is mostly protein with very little fat. A 3 oz serving of canned light tuna in water has about 17 grams of protein for roughly 75 calories. The type of tuna matters most for mercury. Canned light tuna, which includes skipjack, is on the FDA's Best Choices list, the same list as salmon, sardines and shrimp. Canned albacore, also sold as "solid white," has close to three times the mercury, so the FDA and EPA chart puts it in the Good Choices group, at about 1 serving a week. Bigeye tuna is on the list to avoid. You rarely see it in cans, but it can show up as tuna steaks or "ahi" at sushi counters. Salt is the part many people miss. Regular canned tuna has a fair amount of sodium, and albacore has more than light tuna. The "no salt added" kind has far less, so it's an easy swap on the shelf. Mayo, pickles, crackers and bread add even more, so check the sodium line on the Nutrition Facts panel. One more honest note: light tuna is a lean fish, so it has far less omega-3 than salmon or sardines. Think of it as lean protein, and let the fatty fish do the omega-3 work. If you have high blood pressure, kidney or heart problems, diabetes, or you take medicine, talk with your doctor or pharmacist before you change how you eat.

recipe.title: Garlic lemon shrimp with white beans and spinach
recipe.method: Pat 3/4 pound of peeled shrimp dry and season with black pepper. Warm 2 tablespoons of olive oil in a large frying pan over medium heat. Add 3 sliced garlic cloves and cook for about 30 seconds, until you can smell them. Add the shrimp in a single layer and cook for 2 minutes on each side, until pink and opaque. Move the shrimp to a plate. In the same pan, add one can of white beans, drained and rinsed, and let them warm for 2 to 3 minutes. Stir in 3 big handfuls of baby spinach and cook until it wilts, about 1 minute. Return the shrimp to the pan, squeeze in the juice of half a lemon, and toss everything together. Taste before adding any salt. Serve in bowls, with a little chopped parsley on top if you have it.

tip.title: Rinse your canned beans
tip.text: Canned beans are a handy pantry item, but the liquid in the can is salty. Pour the beans into a colander and rinse them under cold water for a minute before you cook. It's a quick way to take some of the salt off. If you see a "no salt added" version at the store, it's worth a look too.
